body.heading: Real jobs, not pretend ones
paragraphs: Children can tell the difference between a real job and a made-up one, and they rise to the real kind. Watering plants, feeding a pet with supervision, sorting cutlery, matching socks, carrying their own bag, wiping the table — all genuinely need doing, and all can be done by small hands.

Size the job to the child, not the other way round: a small watering can, a low hook for their coat, a stool that makes the sink reachable. The right tools turn 'helping' from a performance into a contribution.

body.heading: Slower now, faster later
paragraphs: Helping takes longer at first, and the results are imperfect: the table is wiped in spirals, the socks are matched by optimism. That is the tuition fee. A child who helps at four is a housemate who cooks at fourteen.
Resist redoing their work in front of them. If the standard truly matters — a laid table for guests — do that job together next time rather than correcting this one in silence.

body.heading: Thank the contribution, specifically
paragraphs: 'The plants are happy' and 'dinner was quicker because you set the table' land better than a general 'good job'. Naming what their work changed teaches them that effort is visible — which is most of what any of us want to hear.
Rotate the jobs sometimes so everyone learns every task. The goal is a household where helping is normal, noticed, and shared — not one child's permanent department.

description: Children who are given real, right-sized jobs around the home become people who notice what needs doing.
